questions.question: What is the Divide and Conquer paradigm?
options: An approach that tries all possible solutions exhaustively
A problem-solving strategy that breaks a problem into smaller subproblems, solves each recursively, and combines results
A technique that uses memoization to avoid duplicate computations
A method that always selects the locally optimal choice at each step
questions.explanation: Divide and Conquer splits a problem into smaller, independent subproblems, solves them recursively, and merges the solutions to get the final answer.

questions.question: What are the three steps of Divide and Conquer?
options: Initialize, Loop, Return
Search, Sort, Merge
Divide (split), Conquer (solve recursively), Combine (merge results)
Compare, Swap, Repeat
questions.explanation: Every Divide and Conquer algorithm follows three phases: Divide the problem into subproblems, Conquer by solving each recursively, and Combine the sub-solutions into a final answer.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of this Binary Search implementation?
options: O(n) — visits every element in the worst case
O(n²) — two pointer variables cause quadratic growth
O(log n) — the search space is halved each iteration
O(1) — returns immediately when mid matches
questions.explanation: Each iteration halves the remaining search space (left–right range). Starting from n elements, after k iterations there are n/2ᵏ remaining — so at most log₂(n) iterations are needed.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of Binary Search?
options: O(n) — linear
O(n²) — quadratic
O(1) — constant
O(log n) — logarithmic
questions.explanation: Binary Search is O(log n) because at each step it halves the search space, meaning for n=1,000,000 it needs only about 20 comparisons.

questions.code:
arr = [1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13]
target = 6
result = binary_search(arr, target)  # returns -1

arr2 = [9, 3, 1, 7, 5, 13, 11]  # unsorted
result2 = binary_search(arr2, target)  # unpredictable!
questions.question: Why does Binary Search on arr2 produce unreliable results?
options: Because arr2 has an odd number of elements
Because Binary Search requires a sorted array — the midpoint comparison logic only works correctly when elements are in order
Because target=6 is not in either array
Because Binary Search only works with even-length arrays
questions.explanation: Binary Search relies on sorted order to decide which half to discard. On unsorted data, discarding a half based on midpoint comparison may eliminate the actual target — producing incorrect results.

questions.question: What is the formula for the mathematical midpoint in Binary Search?
options: mid = left + right
mid = (left + right) // 2
mid = right - left
mid = left * right // 2
questions.explanation: The midpoint is calculated as (left + right) // 2 using integer division, giving the index of the middle element between the current left and right bounds.

questions.question: What is Merge Sort?
options: A sorting algorithm that selects a pivot and partitions elements around it
A sorting algorithm that repeatedly swaps adjacent out-of-order elements
A stable, recursive sorting algorithm that divides the array in half, sorts each half, and merges them back together
A sorting algorithm that finds the minimum element and places it at the front in each pass
questions.explanation: Merge Sort recursively splits the array into halves down to single elements, then merges adjacent sorted halves back together, guaranteeing O(n log n) performance.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of this Merge Sort and what drives it?
options: O(n²) — two recursive calls per level
O(n log n) — log n levels of recursion, each level doing O(n) merge work
O(n) — only the merge step is counted
O(log n) — recursion depth is log n
questions.explanation: Merge Sort splits into log n levels of recursion. At each level, the merge step processes all n elements total across that level. log n levels × O(n) work per level = O(n log n) overall.

questions.question: Is Merge Sort considered stable?
options: No, Merge Sort changes the relative order of equal elements
Yes, Merge Sort preserves the original relative order of equal elements
Stability depends on the implementation language
Stability is not a property that applies to sorting algorithms
questions.explanation: Merge Sort is stable — when two elements are equal, it preserves their original order from the input, which is important for multi-key sorting scenarios.

questions.question: What is Quick Sort?
options: A sorting algorithm that merges two sorted halves into one
A sorting algorithm that selects a pivot element and partitions the array into elements smaller and larger than the pivot, then sorts each part recursively
A sorting algorithm that scans sequentially to find out-of-order pairs
A sorting algorithm that builds the sorted output one element at a time by insertion
questions.explanation: Quick Sort selects a pivot, partitions elements around it, and recursively sorts each partition — achieving O(n log n) average case performance.

    pivot = arr[low]   # always choose first element as pivot
    # ... partitioning logic ...

# Called on: arr = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]  (already sorted)
questions.question: What problem does this pivot selection cause on the already-sorted input?
options: No problem — Quick Sort always runs in O(n log n)
The pivot is always the smallest element, creating maximally unbalanced partitions of size 0 and n-1 each time, degrading to O(n²)
Sorted input always gives the best case O(n) for Quick Sort
The pivot selection makes no difference to performance
questions.explanation: Choosing the first element as pivot on sorted data always selects the minimum — one partition gets 0 elements and the other gets n-1, making the recursion depth n instead of log n and degrading to O(n²).

questions.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of Quick Sort?
options: O(n log n) — same as average case
O(n) — linear
O(n²) — quadratic, when pivot selection consistently results in unbalanced partitions
O(log n) — logarithmic
questions.explanation: Quick Sort degrades to O(n²) when the pivot is always the smallest or largest element (e.g., sorted array with first-element pivot), creating maximally unbalanced partitions.

questions.question: How does partitioning work in Quick Sort?
options: By merging two pre-sorted halves into one array
By finding the minimum element and placing it at the beginning
By rearranging elements so all values less than the pivot appear before it and all greater values appear after it
By comparing all pairs of adjacent elements and swapping them if out of order
questions.explanation: Partitioning reorganizes the array in-place: elements smaller than the pivot move to the left side, elements larger move to the right side, and the pivot lands in its final sorted position.

# Option B: Binary Search  
left, right = 0, len(arr) - 1
while left <= right:           # up to ~20 steps
    mid = (left + right) // 2

questions.question: For n=1,000,000, approximately how many steps does each option take?
options: Option A: ~500,000 steps average; Option B: ~20 steps — Binary Search is about 25,000x faster
They take the same number of steps for large inputs
Option A: 1,000 steps; Option B: 100 steps
Option B always takes exactly 2 steps regardless of n
questions.explanation: Linear Search averages n/2 = 500,000 steps. Binary Search takes at most log₂(1,000,000) ≈ 20 steps. This dramatic difference is why O(log n) vs O(n) matters enormously at scale.

questions.question: Why is O(n log n) superior to O(n²)?
options: O(n log n) always uses less memory than O(n²)
O(n log n) grows much more slowly than O(n²) for large n, making it far more scalable
O(n log n) algorithms are always easier to implement
O(n²) is actually faster for most real-world input sizes
questions.explanation: For n=1,000,000: O(n log n) ≈ 20,000,000 operations vs O(n²) = 1,000,000,000,000 operations — O(n log n) is orders of magnitude faster at scale.
